_comment: Recommended remediation per finding category (keys = categories written by RansomwareChecker.ps1). Used for Remediation\<PC>_<time>emediation.html/.md and in the app detail. Order: preserve evidence, containment, eradication, recovery, post-incident. <item> in a step is replaced by the finding item. Always validate a finding and preserve evidence before removing anything.

Evidence: Preserve evidence BEFORE cleaning: memory dump (FTK Imager / Magnet RAM Capture) and a triage collection (KAPE targets: EventLogs, RegistryHives, Prefetch, $MFT, Amcache, SRUM) to an external drive or network share - never to the analysed disk.
Copy the Reports folder of this check with the evidence; note who did what and when.
Do not delete existing volume shadow copies - they may be the only local recovery point.
Containment: If High findings show an active intrusion: isolate the host from the network (EDR isolation or unplug), if business allows.
Block command and control addresses found in the findings on the firewall/proxy; consider isolating the whole network from the internet when the attackers were inside for a long time.
Block remote access tools (AnyDesk, TeamViewer, ScreenConnect, Atera, Splashtop, SupRemo...) and cloud file-sharing services (MEGA, DropMeFiles, MediaFire) at the perimeter.
Reset passwords of every account that was used or could be compromised (local admins, domain admins, service accounts); reset KRBTGT twice when a domain controller was involved.
Recovery: If you are not 100 % sure the host is clean, reimage it instead of cleaning it.
Restore data only from backups verified to be clean and taken before the first malicious activity.
Run RansomwareChecker again after remediation and compare the reports.
PostIncident: Remove the root cause: no RDP exposed to the internet, MFA for RDP/VPN and all remote access.
Patch public-facing systems (VPN, Exchange, Citrix, firewalls) - especially vulnerabilities giving credentials or remote code execution.
Backups: 3-2-1 rule, separate accounts and MFA for backup servers, offline/immutable copy.
Logging: longer retention of Security/System/PowerShell logs, PowerShell script block logging, central SIEM, EDR/XDR with isolation capability.
Phishing as root cause: user training, mail sandboxing of attachments and links.

Steps: Verify the value: who created it, does the target file exist, is it signed (Get-AuthenticodeSignature)?
Collect the target file (hash it, keep a copy in a password protected archive) before removal.
Remove the malicious value: Remove-ItemProperty -Path '<key>' -Name '<value>' (HKLM for all users, HKU\<SID> for one user).
Delete the payload and its folder (e.g. random folder in AppData\Local used by Emotet) and look for the same file name on other hosts.
Restore defaults: Winlogon Shell = explorer.exe, Userinit = C:\Windows\system32\userinit.exe,
Remove the Debugger value from Image File Execution Options\<exe> (sticky keys / utilman backdoor).
Clear AppInit_DLLs and set LoadAppInit_DLLs = 0; delete the referenced DLL after collecting it.
Treat the host as fully compromised - these changes require administrator rights.
Check the LNK target / script content of <item>; collect it.
Delete the file from the Startup folder and the payload it points to (Qakbot uses LNK files).
Search other user profiles and hosts for the same file name.
Export the task for evidence: schtasks /query /tn "<item>" /xml > task.xml
Disable and delete it: schtasks /change /tn "<item>" /disable ; schtasks /delete /tn "<item>" /f
Delete the executed payload; GUID-named tasks running from AppData every few hours are typical for Qakbot.
On a domain, check whether the task was pushed by a GPO (ScheduledTasks.xml in SYSVOL) - remove it there, otherwise it comes back.
Stop and disable the service: sc.exe stop <name> ; sc.exe config <name> start= disabled
Collect the binary/command line, then delete the service: sc.exe delete <name>
Services running cmd/powershell (Cobalt Strike psexec_psh) or PSEXESVC indicate lateral movement - find the source host via logons 4624 / share access 5140 at the same time.
Legitimate vendor services in unusual locations: verify with the vendor before removal.
Preserve the driver file and its service key (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<name>) and hash the .sys file; look it up on loldrivers.io and VirusTotal.
Check event 7045 / System log for when and by whom the driver service was created; correlate with EDR/AV stopping at the same time.
Verify that the EDR/AV is running and healthy on this and other hosts - BYOVD is used to kill security tools right before deployment.
Disable and delete the driver service, reboot and remove the .sys file during eradication.
Enable the Microsoft vulnerable driver blocklist (Windows Security > Device security > Core isolation, or WDAC) and HVCI/Memory integrity where possible.
Export filter, consumer and binding (Get-CimInstance -Namespace root\subscription ...) for evidence.

Remove all three objects: Get-CimInstance -Namespace root\subscription -ClassName __FilterToConsumerBinding | Where-Object { $_.Consumer.Name -eq '<name>' } | Remove-CimInstance ; then the __EventFilter and the consumer.
Search other hosts - WMI persistence is fileless and often deployed widely.
Inspect the job (bitsadmin /list /allusers /verbose); collect the downloaded file.
Remove it: Get-BitsTransfer -AllUsers | Where-Object DisplayName -eq '<name>' | Remove-BitsTransfer
Block the source URL; Ryuk/Egregor used BITS to fetch the ransomware.
Confirm with IT whether the tool is approved. If not, treat it as an attacker backdoor.
Collect its logs first (e.g. AnyDesk ad.trace / connection_trace.txt, TeamViewer Connections_incoming.txt) - they contain attacker IDs and IPs.
Uninstall it, remove its service and leftover folders, and block the product at the perimeter.
Exfiltration clients (MEGAsync, WinSCP, FileZilla): review logs to determine what data left the network.
Before killing: dump the process memory (procdump -ma <PID>) and note its network connections - keeps evidence of fileless malware.
Isolate the host if the process communicates with external addresses; block those addresses.
Terminate the process (Stop-Process -Id <PID>), then remove its persistence (Run key, task, service) - otherwise it restarts.
Masqueraded binaries (svchost.exe outside System32) are attacker tools - collect and delete them.

WDigest: Set-ItemProperty HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest -Name UseLogonCredential -Value 0 ; then reset passwords of everyone who logged on (cleartext was in memory).
RDP: disable it where not needed (fDenyTSConnections = 1), otherwise enable NLA (UserAuthentication = 1) and restrict the firewall rule to admin networks.
Remove netsh portproxy entries (netsh interface portproxy delete ...) and re-enable firewall profiles.
LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy = 0; deploy LAPS so local admin passwords differ per host.
Export the key for evidence (reg export), then delete it.
The artifact identifies the ransomware family (REvil) - use threat intelligence on this family to look for its typical TTPs elsewhere.
Remove unauthorized exclusions: Remove-MpPreference -ExclusionPath '<path>' (and -ExclusionProcess / -ExclusionExtension).
Re-enable protection: Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $false -DisableIOAVProtection $false -DisableScriptScanning $false; turn on Tamper Protection.
If a GPO disabled Defender (Registry.pol), fix the GPO in SYSVOL - otherwise it is reapplied.
Run a full scan after re-enabling; review the files that were inside the excluded paths.
Re-enable recovery: bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled Yes ; bcdedit /set {default} bootstatuspolicy displayallfailures
Set the VSS service back to Manual and recreate shadow copies / System Protection once the host is clean.
Missing shadow copies on servers that normally have them = deleted by ransomware (vssadmin delete shadows) - restore from offline backups.
Verify every member of the local Administrators group and every recently changed account with its owner.
Disable unknown accounts (Disable-LocalUser), do not delete them before the investigation ends.
Reset passwords of compromised accounts; disable the Guest account.
Log clearing means deliberate anti-forensics - assume compromise of the account that cleared it.
Recover events from other sources: SIEM / forwarded logs, EDR telemetry, logs of neighbouring hosts and the domain controller.
Forward logs to a central collector so they cannot be wiped locally.
Correlate each new service with 4624/5140 events at the same time to find the source host and account.
Check whether the service still exists (see Persistence: Services) and remove it.
Investigate the source host as well - it is the next step back in the attack.
Confirm the account creation / group change with the responsible admin.
Disable accounts created by the attackers and remove them from privileged groups; reset the password of the account that made the change.
Block the source IP(s) and remove internet exposure of RDP - use VPN with MFA or an RD Gateway.
Check for a successful logon (4624 type 10) from the same source after the failures; if present, treat as initial access.
Rename / disable common account names (Administrator) and enforce an account lockout policy.
Logon from a public / foreign IP: treat as compromise - reset the account password, block the IP, check what was done in that session.
Internal RDP logons at unusual times: trace the chain of hosts (lateral movement) and check each of them.
Use the detection as a pivot: check the folder of the detected file for other attacker tools and the time window around the detection.
Verify the file was really removed/quarantined; a detection in ProgramData, Public or Temp usually means hands-on-keyboard activity.
Events 5001/5007: find out who disabled protection or added exclusions and revert it (see Defense evasion: Defender).
Read the full script block (Event Viewer, PowerShell/Operational, event 4104 at the given time); decode Base64 parts.
Extract URLs, IPs and file names from the script, block them and search the file system for downloaded payloads.
If it belongs to a legitimate management tool, document it as a known false positive.
Decode -EncodedCommand values and identify the parent process that started PowerShell.
Block the observed download locations; enable script block logging (4104) if it is off.
Legitimate automation (RMM, management agents) producing this pattern should be documented as a known false positive.
Check whether the task still exists (schtasks /query /tn "<item>" /v) and what it runs; remove it if malicious (see Persistence: Scheduled tasks).
Revert firewall rules changed by netsh/powershell outside of change management (Remote Desktop group enabled by rdp.bat).
Find the script that made the change (staging folders, PowerShell history) and the account that ran it.
Parse the prefetch file (PECmd) to get all run times and the files/folders it referenced - it shows where the tool was and what it touched.
Search for the binary and its outputs (dumps, txt lists) on this and other hosts; the tool itself is often already deleted.
Credential tools (SafetyKatz, Mimikatz, Rubeus) executed = reset all credentials that could have been in memory on this host.
The entry tells which user account ran the program and when - review that account's activity and reset its password if the program is an attacker tool.
Locate the executable (or confirm it was deleted) and collect it.
Copy the whole ConsoleHost_history.txt as evidence - it contains the attackers' exact commands.
Follow each command: dumps created (lsass.dmp), hashes extracted (hashes.txt), tools started - clean them up and reset affected credentials (kerberoasted service accounts!).
Preserve rclone.conf / MEGAsync logs - they identify the attacker's cloud account and the exact files that were uploaded.
Report the account to the provider (MEGA abuse) and involve legal/DPO: stolen personal data may require breach notification.
Remove the tools and block the cloud storage domains.
Identify the malicious GPO (GUID folder in SYSVOL\Policies), back it up for evidence (Backup-GPO), then unlink and delete it.
Delete binaries from SYSVOL\scripts and check every client for the copied file and the scheduled task.
The domain is fully compromised: reset KRBTGT twice, all admin and service account passwords, and review all GPOs and admin group memberships.
Collect the files (hash + archived copy) before deleting; the SHA256 in the report can be checked on VirusTotal (never upload a ransomware sample with victim data).
Review the whole staging folder - one tool usually means more (AdFind outputs, a.bat, rdp.bat, netscan, dumps).
Delete attacker tools and their outputs; reset credentials if dumps (lsass.dmp, ntds.dit) or hash lists were found.
Admin scripts of your own that only look suspicious: document them as known.
Do not delete the notes yet - they identify the ransomware family and contact details; photograph/copy one.
Use the earliest note time as the pivot for the MFT timeline (MFTECmd) to find the ransomware binary and how it was deployed.
Check No More Ransom (nomoreransom.org) for a free decryptor; payment decisions belong to management/legal - decryptors may be broken.
Rebuild affected hosts from clean images and restore data from verified backups.
